newsitem.title: USA: Guinness aims to extend appeal beyond St. Pat's Day.
newsitem.headline: Guinness aims to extend appeal beyond St. Pat's Day.

text.p: Guinness, the creamy Irish stout revered by generations of poets and workers, is expanding its U.S. marketing activities in a bid to spread its appeal beyond St. Patrick's Day.

The brand is sponsoring U.S. concert appearances by Irish musicians Van Morrison, Christy Moore and Shane MacGowan, and is also conducting its fourth annual "Win Your Own Pub in Ireland" contest, among other promotions.

Guinness launched its first-ever U.S. television advertising last October and plans further print and broadcast campaigns this year, said Howard Pulchin, director of communications at Stamford, Conn.-based Guinness Import Co.
Guinness, whose two U.S. brands are Draught Guinness, on tap and in cans, and Guinness Extra Stout, in bottles, also sees a growing vogue for all things Irish.
"Irishness is hot and getting hotter," Pulchin said. "Irish music is huge these days, literature ... and cultural happenings like 'Riverdance' are sweeping the country and the whole world."

The world's best-selling stout has been brewed since 1759 at the St. James's Gate Brewery in Dublin. Industry analysts say Guinness has been doing heady business in the United States at a time when overall beer consumption is flat.

"They seem to have found and pushed the right buttons to get this product growing -- it's a consistent grower," said Frank Walters, research director at M. Shanken Communications, publisher of the "Impact" beer and wine industry magazine.

He said Guinness is growing by 20 percent a year in volume, against 10 percent for all imported beers and total industry growth of 1 percent. Americans consumed about 187 million barrels of beer last year, he said.
"I think Guinness has a bright future in the U.S.," said Walters. "Beer is a mature business. Growth is coming from specialities and imports."

Guinness sold 400,000 barrels in the United States last year. Pulchin declined to reveal revenues or budgets for marketing and promotion, but said London-based Guinness Brewing Worldwide views the United States as one of its fastest-growing markets.
"St. Patrick's Day season is a popular time for the brand -- sales do go up -- but what we have seen over the past couple of years is that it's big year-round now. It's growing."
Pulchin said Guinness' volume in March last year increased by about 54 percent over every other month.
The brand is now conducting its fourth annual "Win Your Own Pub in Ireland" contest, which has attracted more than 155,000 entries in the past three St. Patrick's Day seasons.
Participants are asked to submit a 50-word essay on the stout in hopes of winning their very own pub in Ireland. the promotion has been extremely successful because it appeals to the imagination.
"There are so many people out there who have a dream of just quitting their jobs, moving to a place like Ireland, running a pub, and being part of a quintessential Irish village," Pulchin said.
Guinness buys an Irish pub each year before the contest. Up for grabs this year is a pub called J. Morrissey's in County Tipperary.
"We look for a pub with good trade and turnover in a lively town, where someone can move from the U.S. and have a good business," Pulchin said
In an effort to extend the brand's appeal beyond the shamrock season, the company will sponsor the first annual Guinness Fleadh (pronounced "flaw," Gaelic for festival) this June in New York.

The two-day music and arts gala will feature Van Morrison, the Chieftains, Sinead O'Connor, Christy Moore, and Shane MacGowan. Also on hand will be Irish-influenced American artists, including Natalie Merchant and the band Wilco.
Guinness's U.S. advertising and promotions are handled by public relations firm Cohn & Wolfe and New York ad agency Weiss, Whitten, Stagliano.
